The response-code mapping is in the script header; this is not the authors' stricter Win variable (submissive responses only). Some hyenas appear in more than one clan table. Built by data/competitions/mccormick_mara_hyenas.R (#2673).

Reference: Sangwin, C., & Kinnear, G. (2021). Investigating insight and rigour as separate constructs in mathematical proof. EdArXiv.
Notes: Zenodo licence 'Other (Open)'; the archived repository's LICENSE.md is the MIT License (George Kinnear, 2021). judgement_data_all.csv; script ids mapped to proof numbers so agents are shared across sessions; excluded = 1 for the judges the authors dropped (median time < 5 s). Script data/competitions/kinnear_cj_open.R (#2692).

Description: Go games played on Online-Go.com (OGS), 2005-11-05 to 2021-10-12: 25,492,142 decided games between 690,746 players, from Zachary Vance's 2021 dump of the OGS API. agent_a is black, agent_b is white, and homefield is "agent_a" throughout because black moves first; komi and handicap, both kept as columns, are what compensate that, so read the three together (white wins 59% of games, which is what handicap play does to the colour balance). winner is agent_a or agent_b and never a draw: the source records no tie. Also kept: the board size (19x19 11.9M, 9x9 10.3M, 13x13 3.3M, and 67,120 games on 5x5/7x7/15x15/17x17), the rule set, whether the game was ranked (19.3M were), the outcome as recorded (Resignation, Timeout, "6.5 points", Disconnection, Moderator Decision and imported-game variants) and margin_points for the 28% of games that were counted out. Dropped: 1.37M cancellations, 157,798 unfinished games, 59,145 on non-square or unusual boards, 3,267 whose recorded winner is neither player and 247 with a missing or shared player id. Games the players marked private are already absent from the dump; on top of that, usernames, player ranks, move records, chat and reviews are dropped and the OGS player ids are re-keyed to integers, so no row can be joined back to an OGS account.
Reference: Vance, Z. (2021). OGS 2021 collection of Go games [Data set]. Internet Archive. https://archive.org/details/ogs2021

Notes: Script data/competitions/ogs_go.py, streamed from ogs_games_2013_to_2021-08.json.gz (19.6 GB gzipped, one JSON object per line). Description: Human preference votes from LMArena's text arena, 2025-04-17 to 2025-07-24: 135,624 votes in which a person saw two anonymous language models answer their own prompt and picked one, called a tie, or said both were bad. 53 named models are the contestants, 115,363 evaluation sessions are the raters. agent_a wins 48,559, agent_b 49,782, and 37,283 votes are draws (21,529 ties and 15,754 both_bad; `outcome` keeps the distinction that `winner` collapses). homefield is "agent_b" in every row, and that is measured rather than assumed: slot assignment is balanced (each model is agent_a in 50.00% of its battles), yet agent_a wins only 49.38% of the 98,341 decided battles (z = -3.90), the same figure within matchups. The effect is real but small -- carry a slot term in an Elo or Bradley-Terry fit, do not read it as a home advantage. `rater` is the evaluation session re-keyed to an integer, with `eval_order` giving the vote's place in that sitting (1 to 28); it is a weak person identifier, since 102,166 of the sessions hold a single vote and nothing links two sessions by one person. Also kept, all from LMArena's own per-vote annotations: language (126 values, en 71,169, pl 13,813, und 11,833), turns, is_code, math, creative_writing, instruction_following, and hardness, the count of seven prompt criteria met (0 to 7, skewed high: 30,644 votes score 7). The prompts, the model answers and the style-control token counts are not taken. 10 source rows were dropped for drawing the same model on both sides; nothing else.
Reference: LMArena. (2025). arena-human-preference-140k [Data set]. Hugging Face. https://huggingface.co/datasets/lmarena-ai/arena-human-preference-140k

The card's own license field reads cc-by-4.0. This table carries neither the prompts nor the model outputs, so only the CC BY 4.0 material is used and the provider-terms clause does not reach it.

Description: MT-Bench expert human pairwise judgments, 3,355 judgments by 65 named judges over 80 questions and 6 chat models (alpaca-13b, claude-v1, gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4, llama-13b, vicuna-13b). Each conversation is judged twice, once after turn 1 and once after turn 2, so `turn` is 1 or 2 and a row is a judgment rather than a battle. This is the small, careful counterpart to the crowd arenas: `rater` is the judge label as published ("author_N" for a paper author, "expert_N" for a recruited graduate-student expert), already a pseudonym in the source and kept verbatim because that distinction is informative. agent_a wins 1,293, agent_b 1,282, 780 draws; `outcome` keeps the source wording. `question` is the MT-Bench question id, 81 to 160. No date and no homefield column: the deposit has no timestamp, and on sides, slot assignment is balanced while agent_a wins 50.21% of the 2,575 decided judgments (z = +0.22), so no advantage is recorded. The companion gpt4_pair split of the same deposit, 2,400 rows of GPT-4 judging the same pairs, is deliberately NOT built -- those are machine responses, not human ones.
Reference: Zheng, L., Chiang, W.-L., Sheng, Y., Zhuang, S., Wu, Z., Zhuang, Y., Lin, Z., Li, Z., Li, D., Xing, E. P., Zhang, H., Gonzalez, J. E., & Stoica, I. (2023). Description: LMArena text-arena preference votes, the 55k release LMArena published for the Kaggle competition "LMSYS - Chatbot Arena Human Preference Predictions". 57,477 votes between 64 named language models; a person saw two anonymous models answer their own prompt and picked one or called it a tie. agent_a wins 20,064, agent_b 19,652, 17,761 draws. Two warnings. First, this release has no both_bad category, so its "tie" silently pools genuine ties with the both-bad votes the live arena recorded separately -- do not compare its 30.9% draw rate with lmarena_text_2025's without that in mind, and there is no `outcome` column here for the same reason. Second, there are no timestamps at all, so the table cannot be ordered or sliced by time, and it carries no date column. No homefield column either: slot assignment is balanced and agent_a wins 50.52% of the 39,716 decided votes, z = +2.07, short of the z = -3.90 measured on lmarena_text_2025. Distinct from lmarena_text_2025 despite the shared source organisation: the id schemes are incompatible (ten-digit integers here, UUIDs there) so the two cannot be joined, but this release predates the 2025 window and its 64-model roster still includes vicuna, koala, alpaca and llama-2.

Description: RepoChat Arena preference votes, 3,844 battles between 13 named language models, 2024-11-30 to 2025-02-11. A person pastes a GitHub repository link, asks a question about it, and judges two anonymous models' answers. The contestant is really a pair: each side runs a generating model AND a retriever that chose which repository files to put in context, drawn independently (1,932 battles used gemini-1.5-flash-002 as retriever_a, 1,912 used gpt-4o-mini). agent_a and agent_b name the generating model only, because that is what the vote is nominally about and what the leaderboard ranks, while retriever_a and retriever_b are kept as columns so the confound stays visible -- a Bradley-Terry fit that ignores them is fitting a mixture. `repo` is the GitHub URL asked about, 2,377 distinct projects. agent_a wins 1,264, agent_b 1,343, 1,237 draws; the source's own winner field pools tie with both_bad, and `outcome` recovers the split (717 tie, 520 both_bad) from the separate booleans. `date` is a day, not a time: every source value is midnight UTC. No homefield column -- slot assignment is balanced and agent_a wins 48.48% of the 2,607 decided battles, z = -1.55.
Reference: LMArena. (2025). repochat-arena-preference-4k [Data set]. Hugging Face. https://huggingface.co/datasets/lmarena-ai/repochat-arena-preference-4k
Notes: Script data/competitions/repochat_arena.py, built 2026-10-27. Description: GenAI-Arena is TIGER-Lab's arena for generative vision models: a person writes a prompt, sees two anonymous models' outputs, and votes. The task an arena covers is encoded in the model name and nowhere else, so the deposit's votes are split into three tables (genai_arena_t2i, genai_arena_edit, genai_arena_t2v) and no vote crosses a task boundary. Image-generation votes: 8,094 votes between 28 named models, 2024-02-12 to 2025-01-07. agent_a wins 2,982, agent_b 2,968, 2,144 draws. No homefield column: slot assignment is balanced and the left side wins 50.07% of decided votes, z = +0.10. agent_a is the left model and agent_b the right, read from the record's `states` (the top-level `models` field is empty on every vote). `outcome` keeps the vote as recorded (leftvote, rightvote, tievote, bothbad_vote) where `winner` collapses the last two to draw. The source records carry an `ip` field, populated on about a quarter of rows; it is dropped. Those are private-range (10.x.x.x) load-balancer addresses, so they identify nobody -- and are useless as a rater key for the same reason, which is why these tables have no rater column. The prompts are dropped too.
Reference: TIGER-Lab. (2025). GenAI-Arena-logs [Data set]. Hugging Face. https://huggingface.co/datasets/TIGER-Lab/GenAI-Arena-logs

Description: Annual Computer Poker Competition, heads-up events of 2010, 2013, 2014, 2016 and 2017: 683 matches between 91 named bot entries, each a complete head-to-head result in milli big blinds per hand with the half-width of its 95% confidence interval (`mbb_per_hand`, `ci95`). score_a is that figure and score_b its negation, so the pair sums to zero as in the source. `game` separates heads-up limit from heads-up no-limit and `year` the competition. Built from the competition's own archived results pages rather than the 20 GB third-party repack of 620M hands on Zenodo: a crosstable cell already IS the match-level record the comps standard wants, and it carries an interval that summing the logs would have had to compute. The archived pages also cover 2010 and 2016, which the Zenodo repack does not. THREE-PLAYER EVENTS ARE EXCLUDED and are a third of the archived files: a three-handed crosstable is indexed by pairs of opponents, so a cell has three contestants and cannot be written as agent_a against agent_b. No homefield column, and here that is a property of the competition rather than a null result -- the ACPC plays duplicate poker, replaying every match with the hands swapped between seats precisely so that card luck and position cancel, so there is no side to hold an advantage. No date either: the sources carry a year, which is its own column. Do not read the winner marginal (agent_a wins 479 of 683): a pair is written in the order its crosstable lists the two agents and crosstables are ordered by finishing rank, so agent_a is usually the stronger bot. Agent names are kept exactly as printed, including the tbr/iro division suffix, and are NOT reconciled across years, so 91 names cover fewer real entrants. ci95 is blank on the 101 rows from 2017, whose source is a JSON of results with no intervals; every other row has one.
Reference: Annual Computer Poker Competition (2010-2017). Competition results [Data set]. computerpokercompetition.org, via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine.
Custom License (source): Released by email rather than by a notice at the source, because the source is gone: computerpokercompetition.org is now a parked page. Michael Bowling, who ran the competition at the University of Alberta, replied to IRW's ask on 2026-10-23: "The logs are not owned by the entrants. And the ACPC intended the logs to advance research. Consider them released under a CC-BY license (derivative works such as match-level records included)." That also settles the entrants-rights question, which he raised and answered himself.
Notes: Script data/competitions/acpc_poker.py, built 2026-10-27 from eight Wayback captures whose stamps are recorded in the script's SOURCES table. Issue #2689. Where a year published an `uncapped` crosstable it is used, because that is the union of the tbr and iro divisions in one table with identical values; tbr and iro are not two rankings of one competition, since entrants could submit a different bot per winner-determination rule (hence "feste tbr" and "feste iro"). Where a PDF holds a second crosstable captioned "Crosstable using additional post-AAAI data", the first one, "Crosstable of all matches", is taken as the competition as decided; the script records each table's caption. Cells are placed by the horizontal position of their plus-or-minus sign rather than by counting, so a blank cell cannot shift a row; every crosstable is checked for squareness and antisymmetry before any row is written. Shortfalls against a full round robin are blanks in the source, not parse gaps.

Description: AIIDE StarCraft AI Competition, 2017-2025: 173,155 one-on-one games of StarCraft: Brood War between 55 bot entries over eleven complete round robins. One row per game, written winner first as the source writes it, so agent_a wins in every row and winner is the constant "agent_a". score_a/score_b are the two bots' in-game scores, which decide a game only when it reaches the 86,400-frame limit, so score_a < score_b on 38,384 rows and that is not an error. `competition` separates the eleven: the nine annual competitions 2017-2025, plus 2019um, the AIIDE 2019 "Unknown Maps Competition" run the following week on five maps the bots had not seen, and 2022x, which the results index labels "Physical Hardware Re-run" -- the same eleven 2022 entrants replayed three weeks later on different hardware, which moves Dragon from 3rd to 6th and PurpleWave from 5th to 3rd and shifts win rates by up to 11 points. No homefield column: both bots are given a start location on a shared map, and the source records which LAN machine ran each bot rather than which start position, so there is no side to hold an advantage. Also carries round, map, end_frame (game length in frames, roughly 24 a second), game_end_type (blank for 2017-2018, which predate the column), crashed and timeout naming the bot that crashed or lost on frame time, and race_a/race_b -- the race each bot REGISTERED that year, so a bot registered Random played an unrecorded race per game.
Reference: Churchill, D. (2025). AIIDE StarCraft AI Competition results, 2017-2025 [Data set]. https://davechurchill.ca/starcraft/aiide/results/

David Churchill, who runs the competition, granted by email 2026-10-23: "That seems fine, I would allow this to be done with the following rules: - The source is attributed - Anyone else who rehosts the files must cite the original source - It is not sold for profit - There is a note attached stating that it is not to be used for the training of LLMs", and confirmed 2026-10-29 ("Yeah you go ahead and use it, no worries") after IRW replied that it publishes those rules conspicuously but cannot enforce them on a downloader, and that it reads the fourth as barring training on the data rather than analysis of it. Those four rules are the licence. IRW asked him to post them on the results pages; he did not, so this email is the only record of the terms and they are reproduced here and in the processing notes. Notes: Built by data/competitions/aiide_starcraft.py from one detailed_results.txt per competition. Which games count is the site's own rule: "Only games in which at least one bot ended the game 'normally' and counted a final game frame greater than zero ... are counted in the results summary". The two end types the legend marks "No (Winner/Loser is arbitrary)" -- GAME_STATE_NOT_UPDATED_60S_BOTH_BOTS and NO_REPORT, 90 games -- are dropped outright, because this table carries the outcome in the column order and an arbitrary winner would be indistinguishable from a real one; 2017 and 2018 predate the column, so a few are presumably still in. 578 games that reached no frame and scored nothing are dropped too. BlueBlueSky and ISAMind play 2,600 games each in the 2018 file and are absent from the 2018 standings entirely; their 5,100 rows are excluded, following the source, on the mechanism the 2026 notes.txt documents for a disqualified bot ("all of its games purged from the official results"). VALIDATED against the organiser's own published standings (results_summary_json.js), which give per-bot games/wins/losses/crashes/timeouts and a full per-pair matrix: every number is reproduced exactly for 2017, 2019, 2019um, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2025, and for 2018, 2022x, 2023 and 2024 this table holds 10 games more, in 9 pairs, where the detailed file has a contiguous rounds 0..N and the published aggregate counts N. It is never short of a published count. Dropped from the source: the LAN addresses of the two machines, and the six frame-timeout counts (W55...L10000), since `timeout` already names the bot that lost on time. Bot names are the source's and are not reconciled across years (McRave/McRaveZ are one bot renamed); from 2026 the competition assigns random in-game aliases. 2026 is not here: it was still being run at build time. AIIDE 2015 and 2016 publish a detailed_results.txt but no standings to check it against; 2010-2014 publish no game-level file. The core format validator does not apply to this family (no comps profile exists). Issue #2680.
